strengths: MotionLLaMA addresses a meaningful computer-vision problem: jointly generating and interpreting full-body motion across text, audio, single-person, and interaction settings. Supporting nine tasks within a common token-based framework is potentially useful for animation and multimodal motion interfaces.

The HoMi tokenizer is the strongest technical contribution. Table 5 reports single-codebook reconstruction accuracy close to six-codebook RVQ: overall MPJPE is 0.0526 versus 0.0529. Table 9 supports both separate hand/body encoding and frequency-aware gating, with the larger gain coming from separate encoding.

Several downstream results are encouraging. Motion-to-text retrieval improves over MotionGPT, interaction text-to-motion improves semantic alignment over InterGen, and motion in-betweening reduces ADE from 0.3496 to 0.2521 relative to MotionGPT. FineDance generation also achieves the best reported kinetic FID.

MotionHub offers potentially valuable data integration, including coordinate standardization, manual filtering, and additional captions. The supplement provides source-dataset statistics, representation comparisons, codebook-size experiments, and task-specific metric descriptions.
weaknesses: The evaluation protocol is insufficiently specified to establish generalization. Neither the main paper nor supplement provides explicit training/validation/test splits, held-out sample counts, or a deduplication and grouping policy across constituent datasets. This is particularly consequential because interaction sequences are also converted into single-person examples. Related versions must remain in the same split. The training partitions of the learned TMR and gesture evaluators are also unclear. These omissions prevent ruling out contamination; they do not establish that contamination occurred.

The central unified-model claim is not clearly demonstrated. Section 4.1 introduces both two-task expert models and an all-task unified model, but the result tables label every proposed result simply 'MotionLLaMA.' It is therefore unclear whether one checkpoint achieves the reported breadth. A clearly identified unified-model evaluation and an expert-versus-unified comparison are needed to establish the multitask contribution and its tradeoffs.

Several performance claims overstate the evidence. Interaction text-to-motion FID is 0.1133 versus InterGen's 0.0537 despite better alignment. On AIST++, kinetic FID is 58.56 versus M3GPT's 24.34, which is not merely 'slightly higher.' Speech-to-gesture FGD is 194.68 versus MCM's 146.01. Interaction captioning also trails TM2T on BLEU-4 and CIDEr-D. A unified system need not win every metric, but the broad SOTA/comparability claims should acknowledge these substantial tradeoffs.

The algorithmic contribution is incompletely specified and only locally validated. Frequency-aware gating lacks a precise mathematical definition, including treatment of complex FFT outputs and construction/application of the gate. Tokenizer losses and substantial architecture/training details are missing. Reconstruction ablations support the components, but no downstream ablation establishes whether HoMi improves generation or comprehension over a matched conventional tokenizer. Claimed efficiency advantages over RVQ are not measured.

The music-generation evidence establishes rhythmic alignment rather than overall music quality. There is no perceptual or acoustic-quality evaluation, and the supplement defines beat coverage as Bk/Bm, which is not inherently bounded by one. Table 7 also gives M3GPT an F1 of 94.9 despite component scores of 93.6 and 94.0, inconsistent with the stated harmonic-mean formula. The metric implementation and comparison provenance need clarification.

Reproducibility and the dataset contribution require stronger documentation. The exact LLaMA model size, batch/context lengths, task-sampling strategy, motion-completion masking protocol, and baseline adaptation details are absent. MotionHub annotation quality is not quantitatively audited, source counts are not clearly reconciled with the headline totals, and redistribution permissions are unspecified. These gaps matter because the newly assembled dataset and retrained evaluators underpin most comparisons. Overall, the promising tokenizer and task breadth do not yet outweigh the uncertainty in the central experimental case.

strengths: The framework addresses a meaningful and broad motion-modeling problem: nine tasks spanning text, audio, single-person motion, and two-person interactions. This integration has practical value even without leading every benchmark.

HoMi provides promising reconstruction results. Table 5 reports MPJPE of 0.0526 with one codebook versus 0.0529 for six-codebook RVQ. Table 9 supports the contributions of separate hand/body encoders and frequency-aware gating, with the larger improvement coming from separate encoders.

There are credible task-specific gains: stronger motion-caption retrieval in Table 2, improved interaction text-motion alignment in Table 3, and lower displacement errors for motion prediction and in-betweening in Table 4.

MotionHub's harmonization, filtering, and caption enrichment of heterogeneous datasets could be a useful community resource. The supplement describes its constituent datasets and several preprocessing decisions.
weaknesses: The evaluation protocol is insufficiently specified. Neither the main paper nor supplement establishes train/validation/test splits, preservation of source-dataset splits, or overlap controls across aggregated datasets and single-person motions derived from interactions. The learned TMR evaluators are described as trained on MotionHub without specifying their training partition. This does not establish leakage, but it prevents verification that the reported results measure held-out generalization.

The central unified-model claim is ambiguous experimentally. Section 4.1 introduces both task-pair expert models and a unified model, but the tables do not identify which supplies the reported results or compare them. There are no controlled experiments separating the effects of joint training, the larger language model, unconditional pretraining, and additional data.

Several headline claims overstate the results. Interaction text-to-motion FID is 0.1133 versus InterGen's 0.0537 despite improved alignment. On AIST++, music-to-dance FID is 58.56 versus M3GPT's 24.34, which is substantially worse rather than 'slightly higher.' Speech-to-gesture FGD is 194.68 versus MCM's 146.01. These tradeoffs are compatible with a valuable unified system, but do not support the paper's broad SOTA/comparable-to-SOTA characterization.

Dance-to-music evaluation establishes only beat alignment, not musical quality or diversity. Moreover, Table 7 is internally inconsistent with the stated harmonic-mean formula: M3GPT's BCS/BHS of 93.6/94.0 cannot yield F1 of 94.9. The reported MotionLLaMA beat scores are encouraging, but the evaluation does not substantiate general superiority in music generation.

The tokenizer is under-specified and incompletely validated downstream. The paper lacks precise treatment of complex FFT outputs and gating operations, tokenizer training losses, and sufficient architectural details. Reconstruction ablations do not show whether HoMi improves downstream generation over a controlled alternative, while claimed computational advantages lack timing or memory measurements.

Reproducibility and dataset validation remain limited. The exact LLaMA model size, batch sizes, task sampling, and motion-completion conditioning protocol are unspecified. MotionHub lacks quantitative annotation-quality checks and clear reconciliation of the main-text counts with Table 10. No uncertainty estimates are reported, making small improvements difficult to assess. These evidence gaps, rather than the absence of universal benchmark dominance, motivate the weak-reject recommendation.

strengths: MotionLLaMA addresses a valuable unification problem: nine tasks spanning motion, text, and audio, including hand motion and two-person interactions. This breadth is a meaningful contribution beyond optimizing a single benchmark.

The HoMi tokenizer has promising quantitative support. Table 5 reports all-joint MPJPE of 0.0526, comparable to six-codebook RVQ at 0.0529. Table 9 supports both separate hand/body encoders and frequency-aware gating, while the supplementary experiments examine representation and codebook choices.

Several task results are encouraging: motion captioning improves substantially over MotionGPT on retrieval and most language metrics; interaction generation improves semantic alignment; and motion in-betweening reduces ADE from 0.3496 to 0.2521 relative to MotionGPT.

MotionHub's aggregation, normalization, filtering, and additional annotations could provide a useful resource. Retraining text–motion baselines on the common representation is also a constructive effort toward comparable evaluation.
weaknesses: The evaluation protocol is insufficiently specified. Neither the main paper nor supplement clearly defines train/validation/test splits, test-set sizes, or separation of evaluation-encoder training from test data. Aggregating overlapping motion sources and deriving single-person examples from interaction sequences makes source-level deduplication and split preservation especially important. This does not establish leakage, but it prevents confidence in the reported generalization results.

The central unified-model claim is not clearly demonstrated. Section 4.1 introduces both two-task expert models and an all-task unified model, but the tables label results only as MotionLLaMA. Separate reporting is necessary to establish that one checkpoint achieves the claimed breadth and to quantify interference or transfer between tasks. No downstream ablations isolate the effects of joint training, unconditional pretraining, or the proposed tokenizer.

Several performance claims overstate the evidence. Interaction generation has worse FID than both baselines: 0.1133 versus InterGen's 0.0537. On AIST++, dance FID is 58.56 versus M3GPT's 24.34, a substantial gap rather than the described slight increase. Gesture FGD is 194.68 versus MCM's 146.01. These tradeoffs need not disqualify a unified framework, but they undermine broad SOTA or comparable-performance claims without clearly identified unified-model results.

Reproducibility of the main technical contribution is limited. The frequency gate lacks a precise mathematical specification, including treatment of complex FFT outputs and how gating acts on the features. Tokenizer losses and optimization details, exact LLaMA model size, task sampling, batch sizes, and motion-completion conditioning protocols are not adequately specified. Reconstruction comparisons also lack matched-capacity or compute information, and no runtime evidence substantiates the practical efficiency motivation.

Dance-to-music evaluation measures rhythmic correspondence without evaluating audio fidelity or musical quality. The reported F1 of 94.9 for M3GPT exceeds both its BCS of 93.6 and BHS of 94.0, contradicting the stated harmonic-mean formula. This table requires correction and protocol clarification before supporting strong comparative conclusions.

MotionHub needs more auditable documentation: the introduction's single-person and dual-person counts are not reconciled with Table 10, and annotation quality, filtering criteria, source overlap, and redistribution conditions are insufficiently described. Together with the unresolved evaluation and model-reporting issues, these concerns outweigh the promising tokenizer and integration results.
